 NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WZTV) — Millions of Tennesseans are hitting the ballot boxes to pick Gov. Bill Lee's successor after the Republican's eight years atop Tennessee. 
 Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R), Councilwoman Jerri Green (D), David Hatley (I) and Lauren Pinkston (I) sat down with FOX 17 News along the campaign trail to answer your questions about the issues driving your decisions.
 RELATED COVERAGE | Tennessee governor candidates address safety, affordability, schools and more 
 Question: As more big companies and West Coast chains call Tennessee home, some people in Middle Tennessee feel left out. If you are the next governor, will the growth continue at the same rate?
 (See each candidate's response in alphabetical order) 
 “We hear from so many small businesses, and I think what you're really zeroing in on is something that we've heard from some of the roundtables we've done with small businesses," Sen. Blackburn says. "They're saying, ‘Look, growth is good, but we want to make certain that any companies that are coming here are coming on our terms. And that we, small businesses, are going to be able to be in their supply chain, service vendors, so that our businesses are growing.’ And that's what we want to see, is growth that is going to stay here. Tennessee businesses that have, you've got entrepreneurs that have had a great idea and they have pushed that through development and concepting and then they're ready to it to the marketplace. And they are working here. And their jobs growth is here. And we want that to continue. I think there is a...I just have it kind of a little formula that works every time. And it is less regulation, less litigation, less taxation equals more innovation and job creation. And government structures don't create jobs. They should be creating the environment for that jobs growth to take place and that is what our local homegrown businesses want to see. They want to be able to grow to be that mid-size or that larger company and keep those jobs here in Tennessee. I want to make certain we're number one and our jobs growth in rising wages. So that our, that Tennesseans know that they're going to be able to have great jobs for today but also for tomorrow, for our kids and grandkids, so that they know we're the best place to live, to work, to rear a family, to start that business, to retire."
 “I think it's always important to put our constituents, our residents, our voters before corporations and billionaires," Councilwoman Green says. "So I'm the only candidate that's been out actually talking to people and taking their questions, listening to them and showing them I have a platform and plans to make sure their voice is heard, that they are at the table and have equal, if not more of a voice, in what government does. While I do want to see our state continue to grow, not at the expense of families, not at expense of the people who live here, and I want you to know that when I get elected, I will make sure that we take your concerns to heart."
 “I think we need to really start planning the growth," Hatley says. "I think that's what I see. I see not a lot, the infrastructure is really the issue I see in Nashville. When I come down to the Titans games, I'm a season ticket holder there, so the traffic, even on a Sunday afternoon, is crazy getting into Nashville. I mean, getting into Nashville on a Sunday. So, I don't think we have a plan right now. I know that we have the choice lanes program that we're talking about doing, but that concerns me because it's failed in a couple of other states. There are a couple states that the operators went bankrupt. North Carolina tried to get out of that. So, I don't know that that's the answer to our...I haven't seen the contract enough to make a decision, but I think we've really gotta get a team of transportation engineers together and we really gotta figure out what Nashville looks like in 25 years because the growth of this city is phenomenal and I don't see that stopping any time soon. It's a great place. Tennessee's a good place. So, I wanna make sure we have plans in place that we make smart decisions when we're adding to our infrastructure."
 “I think people's concerns are warranted," Pinkston says. "We've grown 14% over the last decade. I grew up in rural West Tennessee and for those of us who have traced our lineage back, generations in the state, the hard work that we're putting in now can't sustain our livelihood in the state anymore. So, I think those concerns are warranted. We know that Silicon Valley is leaving California and is coming to Texas, Tennessee and Florida because of our tax havens. And what I don't see in fiscal responsibility in the Republican party right now is actual protections for people here, right? We have courted large corporations in coming here when they're already benefiting from our tax haven and we've gotta crack down on that."
